prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms made frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep the optical lattice clock as the whole prize, and I do not change my configuration. The question I would put to myself is what nature told us that we did not know. The answer here is a measured one: neutral atoms held in a magic-wavelength lattice, so that the trapping light does not shift the clock transition, can be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free in large numbers, and independent laboratories now compare such clocks at the 1e-18 level and find that they agree. That agreement between separate machines is what convinces me, because it is exactly the kind of check I look for, and it is also where atomic theory meets the experiment: magic wavelengths, polarizabilities and blackbody shifts are quantities that many-body calculations are asked to supply, and the experiments have tested our understanding of them. The physical reach is real: gravitational redshift over centimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a coming redefinition of the second. The credit is compact, with Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking it to record accuracy and for the many-body clock physics. I am also now less willing to pair it with anything, since the only second part with real support in the room, B019, depends on a one-name credit that no one, including its own supporters, can defend.
statement.case_against: The weakest point remains lineage. The 2005 prize gave the comb and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, including the ion optical clock, and a committee could say that the lattice clock is the best instrument in an honoured line whose largest payoffs (a new second, a dark-matter signal) are still ahead of us. I have tried to answer this for myself and I think the lattice concept is distinct, but that is my judgement as a theorist and not something anyone has yet shown against the wording of the 2005 and 2012 citations. Second, the credit has a tail: Ye's name rests partly on record accuracy rather than the original idea, which Olsson rightly stresses, and SYRTE, PTB, NIST and the Tokyo and Boulder postdocs and students built much of the systematics programme. Third, the 1e-18 figures and the priority history are from my recollection and I have not verified them; I would want a short expert note before the final ballot. Finally, there is the timing question, whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Olsson accepts that Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock are the invention, but sees Ye's contribution as closer to a better, later experiment, and asks how far the 2005 and 2012 prizes already cover this lineage.
responses.response: I think this is the sharpest challenge to the two-name credit and I do not want to dismiss it. If the prize were for the idea alone, Katori would be the clear name. My reason for keeping Ye is that the lattice clock only became a scientific instrument once someone showed that its systematics could be controlled to the 1e-18 level and compared against other clocks, and that demonstration, together with the strontium many-body clock physics, is what made it credible beyond one laboratory. That is close to the logic of crediting a concept and the experiment that proved it, as you accept yourself for B020 with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. I do agree that the citation text should say 'invention and realisation' and should not read as a prize for accuracy records. On lineage, I would answer that the comb counts optical cycles and the ion clock controls one particle, whereas the lattice clock opened the large-ensemble regime, and I am glad that you, who ranked it third, say you would put it first if moire materials are judged too young.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene (B020) as a theory-led prediction followed by an unexpected discovery, reproduced by many groups, and names B024 as the honest alternative if the field is judged too young.
responses.response: I have read your case with care, and I defer to you and to Mehlig on the condensed-matter physics. The structure of a quantitative prediction in 2011 and a surprising experiment in 2018 is attractive to me, and I do not think the open pairing mechanism is disqualifying, as I said in round 1. What keeps B020 second for me is the combination you yourself list: a field eight years old, a citation that has to be written around phases and not around an explanation, and the omission of Yuan Cao and of earlier moire band-structure theory. The three-name limit makes that omission hard to justify to the community, and I would not want the committee to decide it quickly. I note that you and Olsson both name B024 as the fallback. If it is a fallback for you, I would ask whether the maturity argument is not already doing the work, and whether the committee can settle the question of Cao first. I keep B020 as my first alternative, and I would move to it only if the condensed-matter members agree that the credit is secure.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs B024 with IceCube (B019, Halzen alone) as a balanced prize of a precision instrument and a genuine discovery about the cosmos, and says a different second part would be considered.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of a discovery in the heavens beside a measurement in the laboratory, and I agree that IceCube opened a new window. My difficulty is the same one that you, Pearce, Kroll and Olsson identify: a single name for a result produced by a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and IceCube builders and analysts left out. You say there is room for two more names, but nobody has supplied them from the shortlist, and I am not able to judge from my own field who they should be. Without that, I would prefer a one-part prize to a second part whose credit we cannot defend, because a weak second part makes the whole prize easier to criticise. Pearce says that B019 should be dropped first and the prize reduced to B024; I agree with that order. I would gladly reconsider if the committee can show a defensible credit, for example a named set of builders and analysts, and an assessment that the origin of the diffuse flux is not needed for the discovery claim.

responses.point: Kroll proposed in round 1 that a short expert note on SYRTE and PTB contributions be obtained before the final ballot, and rejects B036 as a partner for B024 because of its overlap with the 2012 and 2022 prizes.
responses.response: I accept your correction on B036. I ranked trapped-ion quantum computing as an alternative because of the theory-experiment link I value, but the overlap with 2012 and 2022 and the difficulty of the Monroe and NIST credit make it a poor partner for B024, and I no longer see a pairing with B024 that I could accept. I therefore drop B036 as an alternative and use B020 and B042 instead. I support your request for an expert note on priority and on the contributions of SYRTE, PTB and NIST. We both rely on recollection here, and I would put the specific claims to be checked in writing: the date and content of the magic-wavelength proposal, the first lattice-clock demonstrations, and the clock-to-clock agreement at 1e-18.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single quantum systems) prizes; this has not yet been tested against the actual citation texts.

Whether Ye's credit is best phrased around the realisation and record performance, and whether SYRTE, PTB or NIST contributions would justify a different credited set; I have not verified the priority history and would want a short expert note.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, and whether the same maturity standard is applied to B020, where the pairing mechanism is unresolved.
Whether Yuan Cao and the earlier moire band-structure theorists can be handled for B020; I rely on my condensed-matter colleagues for that and for the physics.
statement.conflict_note: I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My close collaborators (L'Huillier, Keller's group, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I work in precision atomic theory, the broad field of B024, and I have supplied theory to experiments of the kind that surround the clock community, which I disclose. I note Kroll's disclosed link to the Hall-Ye lineage and Johansson's disclosed overlap with B042, and I would support whatever recusal arrangement the chair decides.
